blocks.text: Every package in one file, for quick reading or for an AI agent choosing packages for a new game: [packages.md](https://3d.itkamianets.com/packages.md).

items: **Schemas** (5): `3d-scene-schema`, `3d-asset-schema`, `3d-network-schema`, `3d-save-schema`, `3d-inventory-schema`. Plain JSON, readable without Unity.
**Core** (6): `3d-unity-core`, `-scene`, `-input`, `-character`, `-assets`, `-audio`. What every 3D game in Unity needs.

**Game kit** (8): `3d-unity-ui`, `-save`, `-synth`, `-graybox`, `-shell`, `-account`, `-update`, `-net`. What a shipped game repeats: screens built in code, saves, generated sounds, scene-builder helpers, and the shared start screens, sign-in, self-update and online sessions.

**Specific** (9): `3d-unity-interaction`, `-spatial`, `-xr`, `-firebase`, `-network`, `-combat`, `-feedback`, `-ai`, `-inventory`. Editing tools, devices, platforms, services, and game systems (combat, effects, enemy AI, items) that only some games need.
**Constructor** (6): the Character View camera, controls and template for first- and third-person games, VR controls for headsets, and the cameras of the Fixed View and Top-down constructors.

blocks.text: The engine targets Unity only for now. The schemas stay engine-independent, so other runtimes can be added later.
Source code lives in the [IT-Kamianets GitHub organization](https://github.com/IT-Kamianets).

start.title: Start a game
start.lead: Clone a constructor’s starter repository under your game’s name, and it becomes your game.

blocks.text: Pick the one that matches your game’s camera. Each has a starter repository in the IT-Kamianets organization:

items: `3d-constructor-character-view`: first and third person, like GTA V or Elden Ring.
`3d-constructor-top-down`: viewed from above, like Hades or Vampire Survivors.
`3d-constructor-isometric`: angled camera, like Baldur’s Gate 3 or Diablo IV.
`3d-constructor-side-view`: viewed from the side, like Hollow Knight or Dead Cells.
`3d-constructor-fixed-view`: cameras placed by the level, like Resident Evil or INSIDE.
`3d-constructor-free-view`: free strategic camera, like Civilization or Cities: Skylines.

blocks.text: Each starter’s AGENTS.md says what to build first for its style.

sections.title: 2. Clone it under your game’s name

blocks.text: The clone is your game’s own repository. Point it at a new repository of yours before the first push:

blocks.code:
cd <game-name>
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/<you>/<game-name>.git

blocks.text: A starter is an empty Unity project (Universal 3D template, Unity 6000.6) plus what every game needs from day one:

items: `Assets/`, `Packages/manifest.json` and `ProjectSettings/`: the empty project, with one scene and the URP settings
`AGENTS.md`: the guide for you and your AI agent: creating the project, packages to add, what to build first, the engine’s rules
`CLAUDE.md`: one line that points Claude Code to `AGENTS.md`
`README.md`: a short start for people
`.gitignore`: Unity’s standard set, editor and OS files, and `Packages/*` (except the manifest and lock file) so engine repos you clone in stay out of the game
`.gitattributes`: scenes and prefabs as text (Unity Smart Merge once configured), art and audio as binary, Git LFS ready to switch on
`LICENSE`: MIT
In Unity Hub choose Add, select your game’s folder and open it with Unity 6000.6. The first import takes a minute; `Library/` is rebuilt locally and never committed.
In Project Settings › Player, set Product Name and the application identifier (`com.itkamianets.<game>`).
The project has no project-wide input actions asset on purpose: all input comes from `3d-unity-input`.

blocks.text: Merge the block from the starter’s AGENTS.md into `dependencies` in `Packages/manifest.json`. It lists every engine package the style needs, including indirect ones, because Unity does not fetch git dependencies of a git package. For Character View:
Unity downloads them itself: there is nothing to clone. Optional packages (multiplayer, Firebase, VR) are listed in the same file with when to add them.

items: **Interface first, then gameplay.** Start with `<game>-menus` and `<game>-hud` for a playable loop, then `<game>-core`, `<game>-maps` and what your game is about.
**Name game packages `<game>-<part>`**, package id `com.itkamianets.<game>-<part>`, e.g. `temnorid-arena-core`.

Game packages live in their own repositories, cloned into `Packages/` like the engine ones, so several games can share one (several Temnorid games share Temnorid packages). While the game is young, keep them as folders with their own asmdef under `Assets/<Game>/`.
Scenes, prefabs that wire packages together, and build settings stay in the game; reusable code goes into packages.

blocks.text: Open the game’s folder in your agent and ask for what you want to build. The agent learns the rest from files, not from memory:

items: `AGENTS.md` in the repository: read automatically by Codex, Cursor, Copilot and others; Claude Code reads it through `CLAUDE.md`.
[packages.md](https://3d.itkamianets.com/packages.md): every package with its purpose, dependencies, install order and git URL, generated from this website, so it is always current.
[llms.txt](https://3d.itkamianets.com/llms.txt): a short index of these docs for AI tools.

blocks.text: If you only describe the game, for example a team arena like CS2 but with wizards, the agent can pick the constructor and the optional packages from packages.md.

The `3d-*` packages are shared by every game, so changes go back to them through a pull request, never as a copy inside your game. Clone the package into your game’s `Packages/` folder: Unity loads it there as an embedded package, in place of its git URL, and `.gitignore` keeps it out of the game’s history.

blocks.code:
<game-name>/                       your game
  Assets/ ProjectSettings/
  Packages/manifest.json           tracked: Unity packages and the engine packages by git URL
  Packages/3d-unity-character/     a cloned engine repo, git-ignored, used instead of its git URL
  AGENTS.md  README.md

items: Clone the package into `Packages/`: `git clone https://github.com/IT-Kamianets/3d-unity-character Packages/3d-unity-character`. Without write access to IT-Kamianets, fork it on GitHub first and clone your fork. Unity now uses this copy instead of the git URL; the manifest stays as it is.
Create a branch for the change.
Open a pull request to the package’s `master` branch. Keep game rules out of it: the change must make sense for every game.
After the merge, delete the clone (Unity goes back to the git URL) and pin the manifest to the new tag.

blocks.text: Temnorid Arena itself works this way: its repository is the game, and `node tools/setup.mjs temnorid-arena` clones every package it uses into `Packages/`.
Pin every engine package to a tag, so the game does not change when a package does:

installation.title: Installation
installation.lead: Start from a starter repository, or install packages one by one from Git.

items: Unity 6000.6
Git installed, so Unity can fetch packages by URL
For room scanning with `3d-unity-spatial`: the Meta XR MR Utility Kit (`com.meta.xr.mrutilitykit`)
For `3d-unity-firebase`: no Firebase SDK; it uses Firebase’s REST API with your project’s `google-services.json`

blocks.text: Without the Meta XR MR Utility Kit, `3d-unity-spatial` still compiles and reports that scanning is unavailable.

Each constructor has a starter repository: an empty Unity project with git settings and an AGENTS.md that walks you or your AI agent through adding the right packages and building the game. Clone the one for your camera style under your game name.
The whole flow, from choosing a constructor to sending engine changes back, is in [Start a game](https://3d.itkamianets.com/docs/start-a-game).

items: In Unity, open `Window › Package Manager`.
Choose `+ › Add package from git URL`.
Paste the URL of a package from the table below.

blocks.text: **Add dependencies first.** Unity resolves a package’s Unity dependencies (such as the Input System), but not other git packages. So add each engine package a package needs before it: every package page lists them under Dependencies.
A typical order for a game:
Pin a version by adding a tag to the URL, for example `https://github.com/IT-Kamianets/3d-unity-core.git#v0.1.0`.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.lead: Layers that point one way, and data kept in engine-independent formats.

items: **Schemas** (`3d-*-schema`): JSON formats for scenes, assets, multiplayer sessions, saves and inventories. No engine.
**Unity packages** (`3d-unity-*`): core systems every game needs, a game kit for shipping one, and specific ones for editing, VR, room scans, Firebase, multiplayer, combat and inventory.

**Constructors** (`3d-constructor-<style>-*`, and the shared `3d-unity-fixed-camera` and `3d-unity-topdown-camera`): one per camera style. Each adds only its camera and controls (flat or VR) and a starter template.
**Game packages** (`<game>-*`, e.g. `temnorid-arena-*`): the interface (menus, HUD) and the gameplay (rules, maps, content) of one game.

blocks.text: Each layer only uses the ones below it, so a fix in a package reaches every game built on it.

items: `3d-scene-schema`: **where** things are. Read and written by `3d-unity-scene`.
`3d-asset-schema`: **what** things are. Resolved by `3d-unity-assets`.
`3d-network-schema`: **what happens between players**. Spoken by `3d-unity-network`.
`3d-save-schema`: **what a game remembers**. The envelope of a save file, written and read by `3d-unity-save`.
`3d-inventory-schema`: **what is carried and stored**. Items and containers, used by `3d-unity-inventory`.

blocks.text: Unity is never the permanent owner of this data:

blocks.code: Scene Schema → Unity Scene → Scene Changes → Scene Schema

blocks.text: Audio has no schema of its own: sound files are assets, and sounds placed in the world belong to the scene.
Movement is shared; the camera style is not. One character serves every constructor, and each constructor decides where forward is.

items: `3d-unity-input` turns any device into actions: move, look, jump.
`3d-unity-character` walks, runs, jumps and handles slopes, with no camera of its own.
The constructor’s controls make forward follow the camera; its camera follows the character.

`3d-unity-xr` and `3d-constructor-vr-controls` do the same for a headset: the headset and controllers become the same `CharacterCommand`, so a VR player, a phone player and a bot all use one motor and one network.

blocks.text: A game is one Unity project for Windows, Android, iOS and Meta Quest. Differences between devices live in `3d-unity-input` (keyboard and mouse, gamepad, touch, XR) and in the constructor’s controls; per-platform differences are settings and small `#if` blocks.
XR stays off in every build except the Quest one. Game code never touches an XR SDK: it asks `XRStatus.IsActive` and reads poses through `EngineInput`.
`3d-unity-network` is server-authoritative: clients send input, the server decides hits, health and score. Two kinds of traffic stay separate:

items: **Per-tick state** (positions, inputs): small binary data inside the networking backend.
**Session messages** (joins, state changes, game events, results): JSON in `3d-network-schema`, readable by servers, spectators and stats without Unity.

blocks.text: `3d-unity-firebase` keeps accounts and stats between matches; `3d-unity-network` runs the match itself.

`3d-unity-net` is the lighter option: a host-authoritative session with a roster, named events, player poses and host-published entities, for games that build their scenes in code and have no prefabs to spawn. `3d-unity-network` is the full server-authoritative layer above.
A shipped game repeats the same work around its rules. The game kit holds it, so each game writes only what makes it different:

items: `3d-unity-shell`: the screens every Temnorid game shares (splash, landing, sign-in, onboarding, lobby, top and bottom bars), in the structure of the Lords app. A game describes itself in a `ShellConfig` and adds its own places.
`3d-unity-account`: the player’s Lords account: a guest or Google sign-in over Firebase’s REST API, remembered between runs. Not being signed in is a normal state.
`3d-unity-update`: keeps the game on its newest GitHub release and installs it silently on Windows. Being offline is never an error.
`3d-unity-net`: a small host-authoritative session over Netcode for GameObjects for games that build their scenes in code: host or join by address or online code.
`3d-unity-save`: versioned local save files, written safely, with a kept backup of the previous save.
`3d-unity-ui`: screens built in code with plain uGUI, placed by anchors.
`3d-unity-synth`: sounds made in code from waves and noise, so no audio files are needed.
`3d-unity-graybox`: stable asset ids on primitives and the Editor helpers that build a first playable.

blocks.text: The shell depends on `3d-unity-account`, `3d-unity-update`, `3d-unity-net` and `3d-unity-ui`; the others stand alone.
Each line joins a package to one that needs it, as declared in each package.

items: Shared before specific: if more than one constructor could use it, it belongs in a `3d-unity-*` package.
Code that two games need lives in a package, not in either game: the game kit exists because every game had its own copy.
Dependencies point one way, down the layers.
Input only through `3d-unity-input`; no package reads devices directly.
No game rules in engine or constructor packages.
Schemas are the source of truth; engine models mirror them field by field.
Optional SDKs (Meta MRUK) never block compilation; Firebase needs no SDK, it uses REST.

examples.title: Examples
examples.lead: Games and workflows the packages are built for.

sections.title: A first-person game from the template

items: Clone `3d-constructor-character-view` under your game name and follow its AGENTS.md: open the included Unity project, add the engine packages, and make the player prefab.
Press Play: `3d-unity-character` walks, the camera follows in first person, and keyboard, gamepad or a Quest controller all work through `3d-unity-input`.
Switch to third person in the camera settings, or let players switch at runtime.
Add your own packages, interface first: `<game>-menus` and `<game>-hud`, then `<game>-core` and `<game>-maps`.

blocks.text: Temnorid Arena is the sample game: mages fight with spells instead of guns. Version 0.1 is a free-for-all deathmatch against bots on Windows, phones and Meta Quest 3; rounds, teams and an economy come next. It is built from the Character View constructor (with `3d-constructor-vr-controls` for VR) plus:

items: `3d-unity-network` runs the match on the server; `3d-unity-firebase` keeps accounts and match stats.
`3d-unity-audio` makes footsteps and spells audible by direction and distance.
`3d-unity-xr` runs the Meta Quest build: the headset camera and hands ride on the same character.
Interface: `temnorid-arena-menus` (main menu, pause, settings, sign-in and stats) and `temnorid-arena-hud` (health, mana, spell bar, kill feed, scoreboard; touch and VR layouts).
Gameplay: `temnorid-arena-core` (combatants, bots, respawns, scoreboard), `-spells` and `-maps`.

blocks.text: A match’s session, its messages and its replay are defined in `3d-network-schema`, and `3d-unity-network` records a replay from the moment a session runs. The schema repository ships one in `examples/arena-replay.example.json`:

sections.title: From a room scan to a scene

items: `3d-unity-xr` triggers a scan from a controller button and shows progress in a HUD.
`3d-unity-spatial` reads the physical room and produces scene data.
`3d-unity-scene` converts it to a scene document that follows `3d-scene-schema`.
`3d-unity-firebase` uploads it, and `3d-unity-interaction` lets people rearrange the furniture later.

blocks.code: Room scan → SceneData → Scene JSON → Firebase

items: `3d-scene-schema`: `room-scan.example.json` and `corridor-scan.example.json`, two scenes sharing a coordinate frame
`3d-network-schema`: `arena-replay.example.json` (a full match) and `join-request.example.json`

blocks.text: Each example validates against its schema, so it doubles as a test fixture.

The Temnorid games are built on the same packages. Their scenes are mostly built in code from primitives and tagged with stable asset ids (`3d-unity-graybox`), and each starts from the shared shell (`3d-unity-shell`), so the menu, sign-in, updates and online play are the same everywhere.

items: Temnorid Craft, Dungeons, Conquest, Arena, Caravan Guard, Hippodrome and Legends: the first games, each with its own rules on top of the shell.
Temnorid Escape and Detective: short fixed-camera episodes on `3d-unity-fixed-camera`.
Temnorid Master: seven trades in one workshop, with generated sounds (`3d-unity-synth`) and a backed-up save (`3d-unity-save`).
